# Agenda

**Tuesday — Meeting 1**

1. Causal reasoning beyond the regression baseline

2. Prediction versus explanation

3. Turning real texts into research measures

4. Sentiment, classification and LLM labeling

5. AI verification and Thursday preparation

Appendix: tools, extensions, references and reporting.

???

1 minute. Follow this order explicitly. Each section has its own explanation and worked example. The Thursday notebook ends at minute 40 so students have 35 minutes for their own research.


---

# Last week’s model leaves new questions

An adjusted regression can describe a conditional association.

A strong prediction score can show success on a defined evaluation task.

Today we ask:

- What would justify a causal claim?

- How can a sentence become a research variable?

- How do we verify AI-assisted evidence?

<div class="student-note"><strong>Three separate decisions:</strong> what we may claim, how we turn evidence into a measure, and how we check the result.</div>

???

2 minutes. Ask for one example from last week: a coefficient, a diagnostic, or a held-out error. Do not turn this into a second regression lecture. Connect measurement choices back to qualitative coding in Weeks 5–6.


---

# A useful output needs a clear claim

**Quick individual choice — 1 minute**

Which claim is closest to your current project?

**Description · adjusted association · causal explanation · prediction · qualitative understanding**

Keep your choice visible. You will revisit it on Thursday.

<div class="student-note">Your claim determines the evidence you need. A prediction claim needs new-case performance; a causal claim needs a design that supports a counterfactual comparison.</div>

???

1 minute. This is a provisional research choice, not an assessment. Students may revise it when their evidence changes. A descriptive or qualitative project does not need a regression or text model.


---

class: inverse, center, middle

# 1. Causal reasoning beyond the baseline



???

Section transition. Time is included in the following content block.


---

# A causal question needs a counterfactual

For the same unit, what would the outcome have been **with** the intervention and **without** it?

We observe only one of those outcomes for that unit.

A comparison group helps only when the design makes its outcomes informative about the missing counterfactual.

More controls or a more flexible model cannot supply that argument by themselves.

<div class="student-note"><strong>Example:</strong> for one student, we want the test score with an AI tutor and the score the same student would have had without it. We can observe only one, so the design must supply a credible comparison.</div>

> Counterfactual  is a hypothetical "what-if" scenario that estimates what would have happened to an economic variable or outcome if a specific policy, event, or intervention had not occurred—or had occurred differently. Because the true counterfactual is never directly observed alongside actual reality, economists use data, experiments, and models to approximate it.

???

3 minutes. Use a student receiving an AI tutor as a hypothetical illustration. Potential outcomes are a reasoning tool, not two measurements we can observe for the same student simultaneously. A comparison needs assumptions about assignment, timing, spillovers, and measurement.


---

class: small

# Real evidence: training and earnings

**Research question:** Does participation in a job-training program increase later earnings?

The historical NSW records compare **185 people assigned to training** with **260 experimental controls**. Earnings are observed before the program in 1975 and after it in 1978.

<div class="plot compact"><img alt="Observed 1975 and 1978 earnings for NSW training and experimental control records, plus two different earnings contrasts" src="data:image/png;base64," /></div>

<div class="plot-reading">
  <div class="item"><h3>Left: change over time</h3><p>Earnings increased in both groups. The training group increased more, so its before-after change alone includes improvement that also occurred without training.</p></div>
  <div class="item alt"><h3>Right: two different contrasts</h3><p>The training group rose by about <strong>$4,817</strong>. In 1978 it earned about <strong>$1,794 more</strong> than the experimental control group. These answer different questions.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>Interpretation:</strong> the assigned-group comparison is more informative about the training effect than the trainees’ before-after change. Historical subset reconstruction and generalizability still limit the claim.</div>

???

4 minutes. Real Dehejia–Wahba subset of NSW experimental-origin records: 185 training and 260 experimental controls. Training before–after change is 4,817 source dollars; control change is 3,288. The observed 1978 arm difference is 1,794. A before–after change does not isolate training because earnings also changed in controls. Cite the author data page. The selected historical subset and incomplete assignment/attrition documentation limit reconstruction and generalization.


---

class: small

# A possible confounder changes the argument

**Practical example:** students with weaker prior preparation may rely more heavily on AI tools. The same weaker preparation may also lead to lower critical-thinking scores.

<div class="plot compact"><img alt="Assumed causal diagram with prior preparation influencing AI reliance and critical-thinking scores" src="data:image/png;base64," /></div>

<div class="plot-reading">
  <div class="item"><h3>Observed association</h3><p>Students with higher AI reliance have lower critical-thinking scores.</p></div>
  <div class="item alt"><h3>Alternative explanation</h3><p>Prior preparation influences both variables. The association may therefore exist even if AI use has no causal effect.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note">A <strong>confounder</strong> is a prior factor related to both the proposed cause and the outcome. The diagram states a possible causal structure that the researcher must justify with theory and evidence.</div>

???

3 minutes. Prior preparation may influence both AI reliance and critical thinking. A survey association can then combine the relationship of interest with selection. Other structures are possible, including feedback from weak skills to reliance. Adjusting for an inappropriate mediator or collider can create a different problem. We do not fit this conceptual diagram to data here.


---

class: small

# Design choices address different threats

Each design creates a different comparison. Its credibility depends on a specific assumption.

<div class="evidence-list">
  <div class="evidence-row" style="font-weight:700;background:#f1f3f4;"><span>Design</span><span>Practical example</span><span>What must be credible</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Random assignment</strong><span>Randomly offer an AI tutor, then compare later unaided test scores</span><span>Assignment was followed; attrition and spillovers did not destroy comparability</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Difference-in-differences</strong><span>Compare score changes before and after an AI policy at one school and a similar school</span><span>Without the policy, the two schools would have followed parallel trends</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Regression discontinuity</strong><span>Compare students just above and below an 80-point eligibility cutoff</span><span>Near the cutoff, students are comparable and cannot precisely manipulate the score</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Instrumental variables</strong><span>Use distance to a training center as a source of variation in program participation</span><span>Distance changes participation but has no other pathway to the outcome</span></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>Method names are not proof.</strong> Researchers must explain why the assignment rule, timing or instrument supports the intended causal comparison.</div>

???

2 minutes. Mention that DiD needs no anticipation and credible comparisons, RD needs no relevant manipulation and local interpretation, and IV needs relevance, exclusion and other assumptions for the claimed effect. Do not imply that naming a method identifies an effect. These methods are outside the 40-minute text lab.


---

# Claim repair — pairs, 3 minutes

A researcher finds that frequent AI users have lower critical-thinking scores in one survey.

They write: **“AI use reduces critical thinking.”**

1. Name one alternative explanation.

2. Rewrite the claim to fit the evidence.

3. Name one design improvement and its remaining limitation.

<div class="student-note"><strong>Deliverable:</strong> one defensible sentence describing the current evidence, plus one design change that would support a stronger claim.</div>

???

3 minutes: 90 seconds in pairs and 90 seconds for feedback. Alternatives include prior preparation, academic motivation, task difficulty, or reverse causality. A suitable repair is an association in the sampled students. Random assignment of access with a later unaided measure is one possible design, still limited by compliance, attrition, spillovers and external validity.


---

class: inverse, center, middle

# 2. Prediction versus explanation



???

Section transition. Time is included in the following content block.


---

class: small

# The aim determines what counts as success

Before choosing software, decide what kind of statement the study should support. The same dataset can serve different aims, but each aim requires different evidence.

| Aim | Question | Evidence to report |
|---|---|---|
| Description | What is present in these records? | Defined measures and sample boundaries |
| Adjusted association | How do recorded variables relate? | Specification, contrast and uncertainty |
| Causal explanation | What changes under an intervention? | Identification argument and estimation |
| Prediction | How well can we predict new outcomes? | New-case performance and a baseline |

<div class="student-note"><strong>One news corpus, four aims:</strong> count risk mentions; relate mentions to firm characteristics; estimate the effect of a disclosure rule; or predict a human label for a new sentence.</div>

???

3 minutes. Explain that explanation can mean statistical description or a causal/mechanism claim, so students must specify which. Predicting a disease from treatment received after diagnosis can look accurate but be unsuitable for an earlier decision. The right predictors depend on when a prediction is made.


---

# A prediction exercise needs a deployment target

A **deployment target** describes the cases the model will face after development. What will be “new” when the model is used?

- New sentences from a similar corpus?
- A later time period?
- A new firm, country, language or source?

The evaluation split should reflect that target.

A random split can put related articles or templates in both training and test sets. The model may then appear accurate because it has already seen nearly identical language.

**Example:** if the model will label next year’s news, evaluate it on a later time period rather than a random sample from the same dates.

<div class="student-note"><strong>Practical rule:</strong> the test data should resemble what will truly be new when the model is used.</div>

???

3 minutes. In Thursday’s corpus, source article and issuer IDs are not supplied reliably. We remove exact normalized duplicates before splitting, but near-duplicate and company overlap can remain. Report the random document benchmark honestly instead of claiming new-company or future-market validation.


---

# Text classification has a different target

Thursday’s classifier predicts a **human sentiment label**.

A correct label shows agreement with that annotation task.

It does not establish:

- a change in stock prices
- the writer’s private beliefs
- a causal mechanism
- performance on texts the model may already have seen during pretraining

<div class="student-note">A classifier can reproduce a coding rule accurately even when that rule is an imperfect measure of the broader concept.</div>

???

2 minutes. Distinguish agreement with a label from validity of the intended construct. Public benchmark contamination is especially relevant for large pretrained models. Classification can still be useful for coding and retrieval when its limits are explicit.


---

# Method choice — pairs, 2 minutes

Choose the main evidence needed for each question:

1. How often do these news sentences mention earnings?

2. Can a model label a new sentence correctly?

3. Does a central bank announcement change market prices?

For each, name one claim that the proposed data would not yet support.

<div class="student-note">First identify the intended claim. Then choose the evidence and evaluation that match it.</div>

???

2 minutes. Answers: a defined text-count measure with a corpus denominator; a held-out label evaluation; a causal identification strategy with appropriately timed outcomes and counterfactual reasoning. A corpus of annotated sentences alone cannot answer question 3.

# 3. Turning real texts into research measures



???

class: small

# Text as data: language becomes systematic evidence

News, speeches, interviews, reports and open-ended survey answers contain evidence that may not exist in ordinary numerical variables. Text analysis helps researchers **describe patterns, compare groups, retrieve evidence and predict labels at scale**.

**One sentence through several approaches:** “Profit before taxes decreased to EUR 31.6 mn from EUR 50.0 mn.”

<div class="evidence-list">
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Read and code</strong><span>Keep the full sentence and context</span><span>A human applies a codebook and records supporting evidence</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Bag of words</strong><span>Count tokens such as <em>profit</em> and <em>decreased</em></span><span>Transparent frequencies, but word order and context are mostly lost</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>TF-IDF + classifier</strong><span>Upweight terms that distinguish documents or labels</span><span>A linear model learns which weighted terms predict a label</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>VADER or lexicon</strong><span>Apply predefined word scores and rules</span><span>Fast and interpretable, but the domain may not match finance</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>BERT / RoBERTa</strong><span>Represent each word using its surrounding context</span><span>Fine-tune contextual representations for classification or retrieval</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>LLM or human codebook</strong><span>Apply written instructions to the complete passage</span><span>Return categories and evidence, followed by human validation</span></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>Start before the algorithm:</strong> define the research question, construct, unit of text, source and validation plan. A more complex model does not automatically produce a better measure.</div>

???

5 minutes. Introduce text as another form of research evidence rather than as an AI topic. Bag of words converts a document into token counts and usually ignores order. TF-IDF reweights counts. A lexicon supplies predefined scores. BERT-style encoders learn contextual representations. Generative models can follow a codebook, but their outputs still need validation. Manual interpretation remains important at every stage.


---

# The unit comes before the algorithm

A **document** is the text unit stored in one row for analysis. It might be a sentence, interview, speech, article or report.

**Example:** to study how presidents frame economic risk, one speech may be the research unit even when software processes it sentence by sentence.

Choose and record:

- what enters the corpus and what is excluded
- the unit and its stable ID
- source, language and available metadata
- the construct you want to measure

A hundred sentences from one speech are not a hundred independent speeches.

<div class="student-note">The same source can produce different datasets: one row per sentence, article, speaker or interview. The unit determines what N means.</div>

???

3 minutes. Link to qualitative evidence and data provenance. Segmentation changes denominators and dependence. If a project aggregates sentence labels to documents, specify equal sentence weighting, length weighting or another rule and test its sensitivity. Protect interview participants and respect source rights.


---

class: small

# Our real corpus: Financial PhraseBank

**Published financial-news sentences with human labels.** Annotators judged whether each sentence was negative, neutral or positive from an investor’s perspective. The label describes the sentence, not the company’s later stock return.

| Stage | N |
|---|---:|
| Original AllAgree subset | 2,264 |
| After 5 exact normalized duplicate removals | 2,259 |
| Training / test sentences | 1,694 / 565 |

Investor-perspective labels: **negative, neutral, positive**. The training set teaches the classifier; the test set stays separate until the final assessment.

Malo and colleagues. Data: **CC BY-NC-SA 3.0**, for this noncommercial class.

<div class="student-note">AllAgree is the easiest subset because every annotator agreed. Strong results here may not transfer to ambiguous financial language.</div>

???

3 minutes. The release README defines the investor perspective using only the sentence. The AllAgree subset has unanimous original annotation and is easier than the full corpus. After deduplication, reference counts are 303 negative, 1,386 neutral and 570 positive. The dataset supplies no consistent document-date field or realized return outcomes. Retain data attribution and license.


---

class: small

# Text representations serve different aims

One sentence can become several kinds of data. For *profit decreased*, counts retain the words, TF-IDF changes their weights, a sentiment model assigns polarity, and an embedding represents similarity to other texts.

| Representation | What it offers | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| Word counts | Transparent frequency measure | Corpus size, tokenization and boilerplate |
| TF-IDF | Weighted distinctive terms | Training vocabulary and preprocessing |
| Sentiment score | A defined polarity measure | Domain and construct fit |
| Human or LLM codes | Contextual categories | Codebook, agreement and errors |
| Embeddings | Similarity and retrieval | Whether similarity serves the task |

Measurement choices need validation.

<div class="student-note">A representation is a measurement decision: it decides which features of language the analysis keeps and which it ignores.</div>

???

3 minutes. Define a token and an n-gram. TF-IDF combines within-document term frequency with inverse document frequency, then typically normalizes vectors. It is not automatically a topic or sentiment measure. Avoid aggressive cleaning that removes negations, numbers or useful punctuation. Preserve original text.


---

class: small

# BERT and RoBERTa read words in context

**Example:** “Operating profit **[MASK]** by 12%.” The words on both sides help the model decide whether the missing word is *rose* or *fell*.

**Contextual representation** means that the model can represent the same word differently when its surrounding sentence changes. This helps with words whose meaning depends on context.

| Model | How it learns general language patterns | How researchers use it |
|---|---|---|
| **BERT** | Hides some words during pretraining and learns to predict them from left and right context | Add a small task layer, then fine-tune on labeled examples |
| **RoBERTa** | Keeps BERT’s encoder idea but trains longer, on more data, with dynamic masking and without the next-sentence task | Use the same fine-tuning approach, then validate on the target corpus |

For sentiment classification, the complete sentence becomes a contextual representation and the task layer predicts **negative, neutral or positive**.

<div class="student-note"><strong>Pretrained</strong> means the model learned broad language patterns before our study. <strong>Fine-tuned</strong> means we adapt it using labeled examples for one specific task.</div>

???

4 minutes. BERT is an encoder model, unlike a chat model that generates the next token. Its bidirectional masked-language objective lets each token use context on both sides. RoBERTa changes the pretraining recipe rather than introducing a completely different encoder architecture. Better benchmark performance does not remove the need for task-specific evaluation. Sources: Devlin et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.04805; Liu et al. (2019), arXiv:1907.11692.


---

The boxplot hides plotted outlier markers, not observations in the analysis. Alphabetic-token length omits numeric information and is only a rough measure.

# TF-IDF makes comparisons more selective

<div class="plot"><img alt="Mean TF-IDF weights for class-distinctive training terms across the three reference labels" src="data:image/png;base64," /></div>

<div class="plot-reading">

  <div class="item alt"><h3>What the pattern suggests</h3><p><em>decreased</em> is more distinctive for negative sentences, while <em>rose</em> and <em>increased</em> are more distinctive for positive sentences. Profit appears across labels, so context still matters.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note">TF-IDF highlights potentially useful differences in word use. It does not understand negation, numbers or meaning by itself, and this chart does not establish causal relationships.</div>

???

3 minutes. Selected terms are chosen by training class contrasts for display only, not discovered independent topics. The classifier’s features are unchanged. A high cell means a larger average TF-IDF weight in that reference class. A word such as profit can occur in negative news about declining profit.

# Human coding challenge — pairs, 5 minutes

**Three real Financial PhraseBank sentences:**

A. “International sales rose by 59.8 % to EUR 1,244.4 mn .”

B. “Profit before taxes decreased to EUR 31.6 mn from EUR 50.0 mn the year before .”

C. “The divested activities had net sales of EUR 145.1 million in 2009 and an operating profit of EUR 8.9 million .”

Choose an investor-perspective label. Underline the evidence and identify any ambiguity.

<div class="student-note">Record the label, the exact words or numbers that support it, and any uncertainty. A label without evidence is difficult to audit.</div>

???

5 minutes: 3 in pairs and 2 for feedback. Source IDs: FPB_0060 positive, FPB_0361 negative, FPB_1765 neutral. A and B state directional changes. C supplies historical quantities without a directional comparison for the annotation task. It is reasonable to discuss missing context, but distinguish that judgement from the published reference label. Turnover means sales, and profit before taxes is a different measure from sales.

# 4. Sentiment, classification and LLM labeling



???

Section transition. Time is included in the following content block.

# A sentiment score needs an interpretation

**VADER** combines a word lexicon with rules for negation, capitalization and punctuation.

Its **compound score** summarizes the rule-based polarity judgement on a scale from **−1 to +1**. Scores near −1 are more negative, scores near +1 are more positive, and scores near zero are treated as neutral under the chosen cutoff.

We classify scores using fixed cutoffs:

**≤ −0.05: negative · between: neutral · ≥ +0.05: positive**

**Example:** a score of +0.44 becomes positive under the ±0.05 rule. The score measures the model’s polarity judgement; +0.44 does not mean a 44% probability of a positive return.

<div class="student-note">VADER is a rule-based measurement tool created for general social-media language. Finance-specific validation is necessary before treating its score as investor sentiment.</div>

???

2 minutes. VADER was developed for social-media sentiment and may mismatch investor-perspective finance. The threshold definition includes boundary values and leaves the middle open. Its neutral component and the threshold-defined neutral label are different quantities, so the notebook uses compound consistently.


---

class: small

# Real sentences expose a domain mismatch

| Sentence | Human reference | VADER compound / label |
|---|---|---|
| International sales rose by 59.8% ... | Positive | 0.000 / Neutral |
| Profit before taxes decreased to EUR 31.6 mn ... | Negative | +0.440 / Positive |

The original full sentences appear in the notebook and source file.

A financial comparison can depend on **direction and numbers**, even when familiar sentiment words point elsewhere.

<div class="student-note">The error comes from construct mismatch: generic positive words can conflict with the direction of a financial change.</div>

???

3 minutes. Both scores are computed from the full unchanged source sentences shown in the prior activity. VADER does not infer financial meaning simply from changes in the numbers. These examples are selected to illustrate errors, not to estimate error frequency. Validate on the complete held-out sample as well.


---

# A threshold can change the measured pattern

<div class="plot"><img alt="VADER scores by reference class and predicted-label shares under two fixed thresholds" src="data:image/png;base64," /></div>

<div class="plot-reading">
  <div class="item"><h3>Left: score overlap</h3><p>Human negative, neutral and positive sentences receive overlapping VADER scores. Many neutral sentences sit exactly at zero, but some negative sentences receive positive scores.</p></div>
  <div class="item alt"><h3>Right: cutoff sensitivity</h3><p>Widening the neutral band from ±0.05 to ±0.20 moves more sentences into the neutral category. The texts stay unchanged; only the decision rule changes.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note">A threshold is part of the measurement definition. Report it, justify it and check whether a reasonable alternative changes the substantive conclusion.</div>

???

3 minutes. The ±0.05 and ±0.20 rules change 36 of 565 labels, about 6.4%. This is a measurement sensitivity result, not a change in the economy. The histogram uses counts and the classes have different sizes. Neither threshold is chosen by optimizing test performance. A larger threshold creates more neutral predictions.


---

class: small

# Evaluation should include a baseline

| Method | Accuracy | Macro-F1 |
|---|---|---|
| Majority baseline | 0.614 | 0.254 |
| VADER ±0.05 | 0.581 | 0.486 |
| VADER ±0.20 | 0.589 | 0.481 |
| TF-IDF + logistic | 0.874 | 0.836 |

**565 held-out sentences.** Settings fixed before assessment.

Accuracy: share correctly labeled. Macro-F1: equal weight to each class.

High neutral prevalence makes the majority baseline look deceptively competitive on accuracy. It receives 61.4% accuracy by always choosing the largest class, yet its 0.254 Macro-F1 shows poor performance across the three labels.

**Conclusion:** TF-IDF plus logistic regression performs best here: 87.4% accuracy and 0.836 Macro-F1 on the untouched test sentences.

<div class="student-note">A useful model must improve on a simple alternative. Macro-F1 matters here because it gives negative, neutral and positive classes equal importance.</div>

???

3 minutes. Majority accuracy .614, macro-F1 .254. VADER .581 and .486. TF-IDF logistic .874 and .836. VADER ±.20 slightly increases accuracy but slightly lowers macro-F1, so there is no universal threshold winner. Macro-F1 averages the three class F1 scores; it is not the harmonic mean of macro precision and macro recall. These benchmark results do not establish future performance.


---

# The confusion matrix locates the errors

<div class="plot"><img alt="VADER and TF-IDF classifier confusion matrices with counts and within-reference percentages" src="data:image/png;base64," /></div>

<div class="plot-reading">
  <div class="item"><h3>VADER example</h3><p>Among 76 human-negative sentences, VADER labels only 15 correctly and calls 39 positive. The generic lexicon often misses financial direction.</p></div>
  <div class="item alt"><h3>TF-IDF example</h3><p>The trained classifier correctly labels 56 of the 76 negative sentences. It improves substantially, but 20 negative sentences still enter the wrong column.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note">Read one row at a time: start with the human reference label, then follow the row across predicted labels. Diagonal cells are correct; off-diagonal cells are errors worth inspecting.</div>

???

2 minutes. Rows are reference labels, columns predictions. Each row’s percentages sum to 100%. An off-diagonal cell identifies a specific error type. Ask which class is hardest. A single accuracy score conceals these differences. Random sentence splitting does not eliminate template or issuer overlap.


---

# An LLM can apply an explicit codebook

A **codebook** gives written definitions, allowed labels and decision rules. An LLM can apply those instructions to a small batch of **IDs and texts**, without seeing the human reference labels.

Require:

- one label per ID, including **unclear** when warranted
- a short exact evidence quote
- valid structured output

Record the model, provider, prompt, timestamp and checks. Then compare a sample with human coding. A fluent explanation from the model can still quote the wrong words or apply the codebook inconsistently.

<div class="student-note">A codebook makes the task clearer, but the model can still misunderstand a sentence, omit an ID or return invalid output. Human checking remains part of the method.</div>

???

2 minutes. The six-sentence audit uses two sentences per reference class, a deliberately balanced mini-set. It is not a representative estimate of general accuracy. An exact evidence quote supports traceability but does not prove that the label follows from it. Treat embedded instructions as data.

# OpenRouter is a gateway to hosted models

OpenRouter is **not one AI model**. It acts as a routing service between the notebook and hosted models from different providers. The notebook sends one request format; OpenRouter forwards it to the selected model and returns the response.

| Step | What happens | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Prepare** | The notebook sends IDs, unchanged text, allowed labels and the codebook | Every model receives the same task |
| **2. Route** | OpenRouter contacts a named model or selects a free model | A named model is easier to reproduce |
| **3. Return** | The model supplies labels and exact evidence quotes in JSON | Structured fields are easier to check |
| **4. Validate** | The notebook checks IDs, labels, quotes and missing items | Invalid output does not enter the analysis |

<div class="student-note">Keep the API key in an environment variable or Colab Secret. Record the actual returned model because free routing and model availability can change.</div>

???

3 minutes. OpenRouter uses an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint with bearer-token authorization. The OpenRouter-specific HTTP-Referer and X-Title headers are optional. The free router chooses among available free models that satisfy requested capabilities, so it does not guarantee the same model on every call. The notebook can instead request a named zero-priced model after checking the live catalog.


---

</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>Illustration only:</strong> this shows the required input and output structure, not a claimed live model result. The audit compares any returned label with the withheld human reference afterward.</div>

4 minutes. Walk from the codebook to the text and then to the structured response. A JSON schema can require the fields and allowed values, but a valid JSON object can still contain a substantively wrong label. The exact evidence quote helps a human inspect the reasoning without treating the explanation as proof. Official endpoint: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with Authorization: Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

# Four checks make an AI-assisted result reviewable

| Check | Concrete action |
|---|---|
| Code | Test IDs, denominators, score ranges and separation |
| Claim | Compare the wording with the actual evidence |
| Citation | Locate the original and check claim support |
| Sensitivity | Vary a justified threshold, prompt or specification |

**Practical example:** when an AI labels a sentence negative, code checks confirm the ID and allowed label; claim checks inspect the quoted words; citation checks return to the original sentence; sensitivity checks compare a justified prompt or threshold.

Keep disagreements, abstentions and failures visible.

Passing code checks does not validate the research design.

<div class="student-note">Verification should use evidence outside the AI response whenever possible: original data, executable checks and the cited source.</div>

???

4 minutes. Use the lab claim that VADER is a return probability as a quick example. A real citation can still be attached to an unsupported claim. One independent calculation can be more informative than repeatedly asking an AI if it is correct. Distinguish output validity from semantic correctness. Never claim that six audit sentences establish reliability.

**First 40 minutes:** guided text and verification notebook.

**Next 35 minutes:** your individual project.

Bring your current question, literature review, data and code.

Your goal is one improved research output, a verification record, and a clear next step for the complete paper.

You may use a quantitative, qualitative or text approach when it fits your question.

<div class="student-note">The guided notebook teaches one workflow. The studio applies the same logic to each student’s actual question and evidence.</div>

3 minutes. Explain that students stop the guided notebook at minute 40 even if optional extensions remain. The class project studio should improve their actual study rather than generate another unrelated exercise. Remind them that Week 14 connects the paper sections into a composite draft.

Run notebook **1**.

# 2. Sentiment sensitivity — 6 minutes

Run notebook **2**.

Compare VADER scores and the two fixed cutoff rules.

Record how many labels change and how the neutral share changes.

6 minutes: 2 to run, 2 to interpret, 2 for a pair check. Threshold changes affect 36 of 565 sentences, about 6.4%. Neutral predictions increase with wider neutral cutoffs. This is output sensitivity. Neither the texts nor underlying financial conditions changed.

# 3. Classification and errors — 8 minutes

Run notebook **3**.

Read the baseline and model metrics, then one off-diagonal confusion-matrix cell.

Inspect one real error sentence.

**Write:** which words support your interpretation, and what the evaluation does not establish.

<div class="student-note">A model score summarizes many decisions. Inspecting a real error reveals which language the summary hides.</div>

8 minutes: 2 to run and inspect metrics, 3 to inspect a sentence, 2 to write, 1 for feedback. Matrix rows are human reference classes. The classifier predicts labels, not prices. Good results on AllAgree historical texts need cautious external validity claims.

Run notebook **4**.

**First:** assign your own labels and evidence quotes.

**Then:** compare with the human reference and local methods.

If the instructor enables live OpenRouter calls, inspect labels and compare the two prompt versions.

If a call fails, use the manual route and move on.

<div class="student-note">Make your own judgement before viewing the reference or model output. This prevents the model’s answer from anchoring your reading.</div>

8 minutes: 2 for initial reading and manual labels, up to 2 for the live demo or manual comparison, 3 to inspect differences, 1 to record the route used. Model calls have a bounded timeout and no retry loop. No fabricated LLM outputs are included. Never hide unclear labels or failed calls to improve reported performance.

Save the output ZIP and your edited notebook separately.

# Minutes 40–45: method choice

Write four lines for your own study:

1. My research question is ...

2. My unit and source are ...

3. My intended claim is ...

4. My method fits because ...

Use the literature and your available evidence. Revise an overambitious claim if necessary.

<div class="student-note">The four lines should form one coherent chain: question, unit, claim and method must refer to the same study.</div>

???

5 minutes. Circulate and confirm feasibility. For a small annual macro sample, avoid many parameters and naive independent observations. For a survey, flag selection and reverse causality. For qualitative work, justify coding and trustworthiness. Students should not force text sentiment into an unrelated project.


---

# Minutes 45–60: one useful project output

Work individually on **one** concrete improvement:

- a clean table or figure with a clear denominator

- a defensible regression or prediction result

- a documented text measure or coding result

- a theme supported by qualitative evidence

Write a short interpretation for the Results section. I will circulate for brief consultations.

<div class="student-note">One well-explained result is more useful than several unfinished analyses.</div>

???

15 minutes. With 12 students, aim for roughly one minute per student while leaving a little movement time. Prioritize blocked or poorly scoped projects. Ask what the output answers and what would change the conclusion. Do not require every student to run a new model.


---

# Minutes 60–68: verify your own evidence

Check your own work:

**Code/data:** one transformation, join, unit or denominator.

**Claim/citation:** one substantive sentence against its actual source.

**Sensitivity:** one justified alternative definition, specification or coding choice.

Record what changed, what stayed similar, and what remains uncertain.

<div class="student-note">Choose a check that could realistically reveal a weakness in your current conclusion.</div>

???

8 minutes. Quantitative options include a documented sample check, functional form, or missingness rule. Text options include threshold, prompt or segmentation. Qualitative options include a disconfirming excerpt, alternative code or reflexive memo. A check should address a real vulnerability, not add complexity for display.


---

# Minutes 68–73: structured peer check

In pairs, give each researcher about **2 minutes**, then agree on next steps.

Ask:

- Does this output answer the stated question?
- Is the claim stronger than the design allows?
- Can I trace the result to data, code or excerpts?
- What should be clarified in the paper?

<div class="student-note">Give one specific revision the researcher can complete, rather than a general judgement such as ‘looks good.’</div>

???

5 minutes. Six pairs. Leave about one minute to agree on revisions after the two short explanations. Give one actionable comment rather than broad praise. Keep student-specific sensitive data off shared public tools.

# Minutes 73–75: save a research progress note

Save together:

- question and chosen method
- one output with interpretation
- checks performed and their results
- one limitation
- the next concrete action

Use this record in **Data, Methods and Results**. Week 14 connects the complete paper draft.

<div class="student-note">This note becomes a bridge from today’s analysis to the written Methods, Results and Limitations sections.</div>

# The OpenRouter demo is a bounded experiment

- Named free model, checked against the live catalog
- Six public source sentences, without reference labels
- One batch per prompt, at most two prompts
- Zero price caps and no paid fallbacks
- Required IDs, allowed labels and exact quotes
- Safe cache with model, prompt, time and hashes

Do not distribute the instructor’s key or send private interviews to a hosted model.

<div class="student-note">The small audit demonstrates a reproducible workflow. Six selected sentences cannot establish general model accuracy.</div>

???

The helper reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the environment, then Colab Secrets. Set RUN_OPENROUTER=True only for the live demo. Availability, access and rate limits vary. The API helper was tested with simulated responses; no live request was possible during authoring because a stored key was not available. Cached outputs, if later generated, are marked cached. Repeated identical calls can still differ because providers and model versions change.

# Named free models and reproducibility

Catalog examples checked on **20 November 2026**:

- `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it:free`
- `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`
- `liquid/lfm-3-1.7b:free`

`openrouter/free` selects among currently available free models that fit the request.

Recheck availability and record the actual returned model. A free endpoint can still be rate-limited or unavailable.

<div class="student-note">A named model improves traceability. The free router improves convenience but may send different requests to different models.</div>

???

The listed IDs came from the public API catalog, with zero prompt and completion prices. The helper also blocks nonzero request pricing and caps prices per request. Do not silently switch to a paid endpoint or describe random free routing as the same fixed model across prompts. Live user-account access remains unverified.

# Similarity is another text application

<div class="plot"><img alt="Cosine similarity among the six real audit sentences using the training-fitted TF-IDF representation" src="data:image/png;base64," /></div>

<div class="plot-reading">
  <div class="item"><h3>How to read the matrix</h3><p>The diagonal equals 1 because every sentence is identical to itself. Darker off-diagonal cells indicate pairs that share more heavily weighted terms.</p></div>
  <div class="item alt"><h3>What similarity means</h3><p>Two sentences can use similar vocabulary while expressing different sentiment or describing different events. Researchers must inspect the actual pair.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="student-note">Cosine similarity measures closeness in the chosen TF-IDF representation. It does not by itself establish a shared argument, cause or substantive meaning.</div>

???

Optional after-class extension. The diagonal is one because a vector matches itself. Off-diagonal similarity reflects weighted vocabulary overlap. It does not establish common sentiment, equivalent meanings, or a causal link. The optional notebook retrieves three training sentences related to one test sentence.

# Other software extends the workflow

| Task | Tool examples |
|---|---|
| Counts, TF-IDF and classification | pandas and scikit-learn |
| Lexicon/rule sentiment | VADER |
| Tokenization and named entities | spaCy |
| Domain models and embeddings | Hugging Face / FinBERT / sentence embeddings |
| Hosted LLM coding | OpenRouter plus validated structured output |
| Original-source and reference checks | Publisher/preprint pages and Zotero |

Choose tools after defining the research task.

<div class="student-note">Choose software only after defining the task. A more advanced model does not repair a weak construct or evaluation design.</div>

???

No additional large model download is required in the 40-minute lab. ProsusAI FinBERT was fine-tuned on Financial PhraseBank, so scoring this corpus with it is not a clean new-data test. Entity recognition and embeddings also need task-specific validation. Zotero stores references but cannot establish whether a claim follows from a source.

class: small

# A verification record should be inspectable

| Item | What to retain |
|---|---|
| Data | Source, rights, document IDs and selection rules |
| Measurement | Tokenization, codebook, score and aggregation definitions |
| Model | Training/evaluation design or provider/model details |
| AI use | Purpose, prompt/version and accepted output |
| Validation | Manual checks, errors, failures and sensitivity results |

A small transparent study can support a clear final paper.

<div class="student-note">A reader should be able to trace a reported claim back to the source records, measurement rule and analysis decision.</div>

???

The final project is individual and complete in structure, rather than a proposal. Students should be able to reproduce or reconstruct the relevant evidence, with a restricted-data explanation when sharing raw material is inappropriate. Do not require all tools or all methods.

# Sources for the real examples

**Causal-design illustration:** Dehejia–Wahba NSW files from the [author’s data page](https://users.nber.org/~rdehejia/data/.nswdata2.html). Actual experimental-origin subset, with stated reconstruction limits.

**Text corpus:** Malo et al. (2013 preprint), [Good Debt or Bad Debt](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.5336). [Financial PhraseBank mirror and card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/takala/financial_phrasebank). Original README and CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 license included.

**Sentiment:** Hutto and Gilbert (2014), [VADER author repository](https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment), MIT license.

???

All empirical figures and numerical results use the documented real source data. The causal diagram is explicitly a conceptual assumption. Unsupported claims in the verification exercise are identified as deliberately written teaching examples.
